title: Simplification, Conjunction and Addition (Simp, Conj, Add)
short: Simp: from p ∧ q, infer p. Conj: from p and q, infer p ∧ q. Add: from p, infer p ∨ q for any q at all.
trouble: Addition feels like cheating, and learners wrongly apply Simp to a disjunction. From p ∨ q you cannot infer p.

blocks.html: Three short rules handle $\land$ and $\lor$ directly. They look almost too simple, but proofs are full of them. They join the rules from Hypothetical and Disjunctive Syllogism (HS, DS).
Simp takes one conjunct out of a conjunction. Conj joins two lines with $\land$. Add joins anything at all to a line with $\lor$. Simp and Add cite one line; Conj cites two.

If $p \land q$ is true, both parts are true, so either one may be written alone (Simp). If $p$ and $q$ are each true, their conjunction is true (Conj). Addition is the surprising one: if $p$ is true, then $p \lor q$ is true whatever $q$ is, because a disjunction needs only one true part. Adding does lose information, but it never takes you from truth to falsehood, and that is all a rule needs.

blocks.name: lg-proof

lines.note: Add brings in r, which the conditional needs.

blocks.cap: All three rules in one proof.

blocks.title: Simplification
blocks.q: From $(p \to q) \land \neg r$, what can Simp give?
steps: Either conjunct may be written alone.

blocks.title: Conjunction
blocks.q: From line 2, $\neg p$, and line 5, $q \lor r$, what does Conj give?
steps: Join the two lines with $\land$, in the order you choose.

blocks.title: Addition
blocks.q: You have $s$ and the conclusion is $s \lor (t \to u)$. How do you finish?
steps: The conclusion is a disjunction whose first disjunct is $s$.
Add may attach any formula with $\lor$.
blocks.a: Write $s \lor (t \to u)$ by Add from the line $s$.

blocks.html: Applying Simp to a disjunction: from $p \lor q$ inferring $p$. A disjunction can be true with $p$ false, so nothing can be "simplified" out of it. Simp works only on a whole line whose main connective is $\land$. The opposite worry, that Add feels like cheating, is unfounded: Add is valid, since $p \lor q$ is true in every row where $p$ is.

items: Simp: whole line is $A \land B$ → write $A$ or $B$.
Add: one line $A$ → write $A$ $\lor$ anything you like.

blocks.html: These rules are also how you take a conjunction apart and put a new one together. A premise like $p \land (q \to r)$ is two premises in one: Simp gives you $p$ and $q \to r$ as separate lines, and then the other rules can use them. At the end, Conj puts the pieces of a conjunctive conclusion back together.
Watch for Add whenever the conclusion contains a letter that appears in no premise: only Add can introduce something new.
